1078825,ca.proc.d.1936-02-21.7.1.2,1936-02-21,ac397c18-e022-437d-b73d-778fbe4a493b,ca.m.6031,Mr. SPEAKER:,Speaker of the Senate,BUREAU FOR TRANSLATIONS,"PROPOSED BILL TO REPEAL 24-25 GEORGE V, 1934, CHAPTER 25, RULED OUT OF ORDER",,"With reference to this bill, I suspended my decision yesterday, and I have considered this matter most carefully and am prepared to render decision in the matter.
There are only two clauses to this bill:

column2: Chapter 25 of 24-25 George V is hereby repealed.
Hereinafter each translator shall be under the head of the department concerned.

column1: Under standing order 76, every clause of a bill must be considered by the committee of the house in its proper order. If clause 1 of the proposed bill were passed, the result would automatically be the abolition of the positions
Bureau for Translations
of nearly all the translators in the civil service, as they have been practically all absorbed by the bureau for translations.

When the house would reach clause 2 of the bill, there would be no bureau for translations. New appointments would have to be made if each department were to do its own translating. Clause 2 therefore provides for the appointment of additional civil servants. Such a bill cannot be introduced by a private member. Its introduction must be moved by a minister of the crown on the recommendation of the governor general, and it must be preceded by a resolution in committee of the whole.

I may quote as a precedent a ruling of Mr. Speaker Rhodes who on May 17, 1918, decided that a motion to amend a bill so as to provide for the appointment of additional government officials is out of order as it involves an increased grant of public money.

On March 17, 1933, Mr. Jean moved for leave to introduce a bill to amend the Bankruptcy Act so as to provide for a joint superintendent of bankruptcy. Mr. Speaker Black moved it out of order on the ground that the bill provided for the appointment of an official and would therefore entail a charge upon the revenue. Such legislation, he stated, could be introduced only by a minister on the approval of the crown.

Another element which places this measure in the category of money bills is that its adoption would mean the transfer of the authority under which appropriated money is to be spent. The translators' salaries have been voted as part of the estimates of the Secretary of State's department. This was done by resolution in committee of supply and it was subsequently embodied in the appropriation bill. When money is voted, the main conditions imposed on its expenditure are embodied in resolutions. All the circumstances concerning its destination form part of the appropriation with which they are considered, and if any alteration is to be made it must be by the same process as the original resolution.

A money bill is defined in the British house as a public bill which contains only provisions dealing with, inter alia, the ""custody"" of public money. The custody is undoubtedly the placing of an appropriation under a certain minister. The translators' salaries, which cannot be separated from the proposed bill, have been placed in the custody of the Secretary of State, and the bill provides that it be given to several other ministers.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier. speaking on an alleged money bill in the session of 1911-12 (Hansard, column 3633-3641), said:

The time when we should dispose of the manner in which the money is to be expended is when the money is appropriated and therefore it should be first of all introduced by resolution where any objections which may properly be urged against the resolution should be urged.

This opinion of Laurier goes to show that the circumstances under which an expenditure is to be made are indivisible from that expenditure. The choice of the minister responsible for paying out the money is a material condition of an appropriation, and in order to change it the house would have to amend the principal clauses of a money bill.
I am therefore of the opinion that the proposed measure has all the earmarks of a money bill and cannot be introduced by a private member. I declare it out of order.

,Liberal,,Walter Edward Foster,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=ac397c18-e022-437d-b73d-778fbe4a493b&Language=E&Section=ALL

1078827,ca.proc.d.1936-02-21.8.1,1936-02-21,,,,subtopic,ELECTIONS AND FRANCHISE,APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY AND REPORT ON AMENDMENTS TO ELECTIONS AND FRANCHISE ACTS,,,,,,
1078828,ca.proc.d.1936-02-21.8.1.1,1936-02-21,4d5012f1-c091-43d5-b8fc-f6f7ac8afb9c,ca.m.491,Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved:,Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada,ELECTIONS AND FRANCHISE,APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY AND REPORT ON AMENDMENTS TO ELECTIONS AND FRANCHISE ACTS,,That a special committee, the members thereof to be selected at a later date, be appointed to study the Dominion Elections Act 1934 and amendments thereto and the Franchise Act 1934 and amendments thereto and to suggest to the house, such amendments to the said acts as they may deem advisable, and, furthermore, such committee shall study and make a report on the following subjects:-
(a) The proportional representation system;
(ib) The alternative vote in single-member constituencies;
(c) Compulsory registration of voters;
(d1) Compulsory voting;
and that the said special committee have power to send for persons, papers and records, to examine witnesses under oath and report from time to time.

He said: Mr. Speaker, this resolution is self explanatory and requires very little comment. I think hon. gentlemen will agree that if changes are to be made in the election laws of the country it is better that they should be made in the first days of a parliament rather than immediately before an election, because then there are suspicions of ulterior motives.

The committee to be appointed will consider the recommendations made by the chief electoral officer and the franchise commissioner and will study any suggested amendments to these acts as they are to-day. That is general. The four subjects which are mentioned do not subtract anything from the general aspect of the question. The proportional representation system is the first subject to be sent to the committee for consideration. This has been discussed and debated in this house on
Elections and Franchise

various occasions, I must say with indifferent success as to the support it has been given. The other method, the alternative vote in single member constituencies, seems to have enlisted more favour on the part of hon. members, to such an extent that at one time or another both major parties have proposed it in some form. As Minister of Justice in a former government, prior to 1930, I introduced a bill to establish the alternative vote in single member constituencies, but the bill had to be withdrawn because it met considerable opposition and would have kept the house sitting for a very long time. Then last year, just before the expiration of the last parliament, a proposal was made in the form of a bill to experiment with the alternative vote system in one province, Saskatchewan. The objection raised at that time was very strong; first that it was late in the day, and second that it was thought undesirable that there should be a special system of voting in one part of the country which would be different from that in other parts of the country. I submit, however, that immediately after a general election is a propitious occasion for the consideration of the whole question of both systems, proportional representation and the alternative vote in single member constituencies.

As to the two other questions that are submitted, compulsory registration of voters and compulsory voting, these were referred to the other day by my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). They are in force in Australia. I do not know that they are applied in any other country. It would be of interest to have the committee study them and consider whether the conditions in that country could be applied with the same success, if there has been success, to Canada. However, I submit this motion to the house, and if it is carried we will select at a later day the members to serve on the committee.

1078833,ca.proc.d.1936-02-21.8.1.6,1936-02-21,b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f,ca.m.6164,Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):,Leader of the Official Opposition,ELECTIONS AND FRANCHISE,APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY AND REPORT ON AMENDMENTS TO ELECTIONS AND FRANCHISE ACTS,,Mr. Speaker, I heartily agree with what the minister has said as to the desirability of a committee considering possible amendments to the Franchise Act and the Dominion Elections Act at the beginning of a new parliament. The hon. gentleman will perhaps recall, as will the house, that owing to the census having been taken in 1931 many matters of this kind could not be dealt with until it was possible to determine upon a redistribution measure. The circumstances in connection with the introduction and passing of the Franchise Act are known if not to all hon. members of the house at least to some; for from time to time we had been endeavouring to secure some form of lists in this country for elections. We abandoned the preparation of lists something like twenty years ago, except just prior to an election, and now that we have reverted to the method that prevails in Great Britain and other countries, the method that formerly prevailed here, I think it is important that we should have a report made to this house as to whether or not this method has been found satisfactory.

As to the methods of voting, as long as the committee has a free hand to consider such methods I do not see any particular objection. The enumeration of three particular methods, with a suggestion as to compulsory voting, may have the effect of directing attention to them only; it will be observed that the resolution provides that the committee shall study and make a report on ""the following subjects,"" and then these subjects are set out. However, from what the minister has said I take it that if it is thought desirable by the committee that the scope of its activities should be enlarged, that may be done without coming again to the house. There is one other matter that I suppose can be discussed without its being specifically referred to in the motion, and that is the date of elections. It will be recalled that as the law now stands the election day is fixed for a Monday, and owing to one Monday falling upon a holiday -not a general holiday as is provided for in the act, but a holiday to certain people in this country-we were compelled to postpone the election for a whole week. I suppose we can consider that as something that arises out of the submission of the franchise act and elections act to the committee.

The minister has not indicated anything as to the number he might have in mind for the committee. That may or may not be important. I thought probably he would have referred the whole matter to the com-
Elections and Franchise

mittee on privileges and elections, but perhaps under all the circumstances a special committee will obtain better results and give the matter more consideration. As long as it is clear that there is no limitation proposed or intended by specifying particular subjects, and that the fullest possible opportunity will be given the committee to consider every matter that arises out of the operation of the franchise act and the elections act. I heartily support the submission of this matter to a special committee.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Richard Bedford Bennett,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f&Language=E&Section=ALL
1078834,ca.proc.d.1936-02-21.8.1.7,1936-02-21,073412d5-f06d-4109-82a1-fb311c3559ce,ca.m.9524,Mr. LAPOINTE (Quebec Ea9t):,,ELECTIONS AND FRANCHISE,APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY AND REPORT ON AMENDMENTS TO ELECTIONS AND FRANCHISE ACTS,,Would

my right hon. friend give me his views as to the number of members who should sit on the committee? I think it should be a fairly large committee, in order to give representation to all the provinces and the various sections in the house-perhaps nearly thirty; twenty-nine or twenty-eight? I am told that the last committee consisted of twenty-nine members.

,Liberal,,Arthur-Joseph Lapointe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=073412d5-f06d-4109-82a1-fb311c3559ce&Language=E&Section=ALL
1078835,ca.proc.d.1936-02-21.8.1.8,1936-02-21,b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f,ca.m.6164,Mr. BENNETT:,Leader of the Official Opposition,ELECTIONS AND FRANCHISE,APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY AND REPORT ON AMENDMENTS TO ELECTIONS AND FRANCHISE ACTS,,As long as the quorum is fixed low enough. It has been found necessary I observe in other legislatures dealing with public matters recently to provide for a small quorum because of the difficulty of getting attendance. As long as the quorum is reasonably low I think a committee of between twenty and thirty would be satisfactory.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Richard Bedford Bennett,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f&Language=E&Section=ALL
1078836,ca.proc.d.1936-02-21.8.1.9,1936-02-21,8844037f-c912-404d-a505-6bf56321dd9a,ca.m.1140,Hon. CHARLES MARCIL (Bonaventure):,,ELECTIONS AND FRANCHISE,APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY AND REPORT ON AMENDMENTS TO ELECTIONS AND FRANCHISE ACTS,,I quite agree with the proposal that this matter should be introduced early in the life of the parliament. We have made many attempts since confederation to get a proper basis; we have amended the law over and over again, both as regards the franchise and as regards the composition of the house. As I see it, there are two most important features to be considered. One is that we have in this parliament a large number of members who represent a minority of the electors in their constituencies. That should be remedied, so that the man who is elected represents an absolute majority of his constituents. The other is that we should aim to place upon the voter a sense of responsibility, a realization that the election of a member of parliament is a matter of concern not only to the candidate, but that the elector himself is called upon at that time to fulfil the greatest obligation and duty which devolves upon the citizen, the election of a government to administer the affairs of the country. That will give the new committee plenty of work, and I hope that a change will be brought about so that a large vote may be assured and that those who are elected will really represent the people of their constituencies.

,Liberal,,Charles Marcil,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=8844037f-c912-404d-a505-6bf56321dd9a&Language=E&Section=ALL

POWER (Minister of Pensions and National Health):,Minister of Pensions and National Health,PENSION REGULATIONS,CHANGES IN MAXIMUM MONTHLY HOSPITAL ALLOWANCES FOR CERTAIN CLASSES OF EX-SOLDIERS,,The reports carried in the press, although quite true, are perhaps of a nature to alarm needlessly the interested parties. The situation is this: from the termination of the war down to the present day any ex-soldiers who were taken into hospital on account of their pensionable disabilities were immediately placed on pay and allowances of the rank which they held during their service in the army. That is to say, a private soldier was placed on pay and allowances approximately equal to those which he received
Pension Regulations

as a private soldier in the army, and a general or colonel was placed on the pay and allowances of the rank which he held in the army. The divergence has always appeared to me to be pretty wide, and after considerable study the officers of the department and myself came to the conclusion that perhaps at this time, twenty years after the war, we should not perpetuate the system of pay according to rank which existed during the war. So that by order in council which comes into effect March 1, an attempt is being made to equalize in some degree the rates being paid. Under the present system, which will be changed on March 1, a private soldier when he goes into hospital receives $45 per month. If he has a wife and say six children his pay can run to $137 per month. After March 1, he will still receive S45 if he is single and $137 if he is married and has six children. There is no change whatsoever made in the rate of pay to private soldiers. At the present time a colonel, if he is single when he enters the hospital, receives $228 a month. After March 1, he will receive $127. At present a colonel who is married and has six children receives $288 a month; after March 1 he will receive S219. For a major general-which is perhaps an extreme case, though if I may be permitted I might say that we did have in the hospital some years ago a gentleman who, at the rate of pay he was drawing together with the pension he received from the militia department, was being compensated at the rate of about S14,000 a year for lying in the hospital with a very minor ailment-

A sudden or drastic cut in their allowances might effect some hardship. We are prepared to go into that question. If it is shown that delay is necessary in order that readjustment may be possible, perhaps that could be arranged. The

other ranks, however, other than private soldiers, will in no case receive less than if they were placed on one hundred per cent disability pension less the usual amount deducted to cover partial cost of maintenance. That is to say, the amount of money which they receive while they are in hospital will never be less than if they were outside hospital on a one hundred per cent total disability pension, less $30.00 per month.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Ernest Edward Perley,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=ec4705d1-ca91-4304-a96d-3a9366b998ca&Language=E&Section=ALL
1078870,ca.proc.d.1936-02-21.10.23,1936-02-21,b88f8c1a-3837-4be1-8acb-61fedd1a9cc1,ca.m.1363,Mr. GARDINER:,Minister of Agriculture,DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE,,,The matter of rust

resistant wheat is something which becomes of interest periodically in western Canada. I remember three outstanding years during the time I have been in the west when we had great destruction of crop as a result of rust, and after each one of those years there was strong agitation for the development of a rust resistant wheat. We experienced very little success in that direction until the last ten or twelve years, during which there has been a decided effort on the part of the department to develop a rust resistant wheat, working in cooperation with agricultural colleges on both sides of the line, provincial authorities and others. A few years ago, I think it was while the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) was Minister of Agriculture, he emphasized the importance of the development of rust resistant wheat, and secured funds with which to set up a laboratory at Winnipeg. That laboratory has been operating since. Certain lands have been set apart on which wheats have been developed. These wheats have been distributed to the experimental farms, at Indian Head and elsewhere, and to agricultural colleges, and certain developments have taken place. I understand that as a result of those developments, there originated three strains of what are generally recognized to-day as rust resistant wheats which are now in the course of development. It has been fairly well established by the experience of last year, when we had one of the worst attacks of rust the west has experienced, that at least three of these strains are likely to be rust resistant. It is not the intention, so far as these strains are concerned, to give them wide distribution until the fall of 1937. Those who are familiar with the distribution of wheats in western Canada will recall that there was some difficulty in the distribution of Reward wheat because of its having been distributed while it was still affected by loose smut. The department is anxious to avoid any such difficulties in connection with the distribution of rust resistant wheat. The wheat will probably be distributed in the fall of 1937, I assume in the usual way, a few bushels being sent here and there to farmers who are interested in having it. They will grow' a crop from it, and that crop will be for sale to other farmers to sow on their land, so that eventually it will be sown fairly widely over the west.
There is a wheat called Thatcher wheat which is being brought in from the state of Minnesota, where it was developed. It is being sown this year by some of the farmers

When the twenty million dollar public works program was inaugurated two years ago I was told by the then Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Weir, that a certain amount of money would be expended on buildings on that farm. I know the situation at that farm and I do not have to go to any officials for information. I believe the officials there are the best in the land. The minister must know the situation. During the war the land upon which the farm is now located was cleared by German prisoners of war. These men were quartered in shacks which at that time were probably fairly comfortable, but some of these shacks are still being used to house the workingmen on the farm. I really believe the cattle are better housed than the workingmen. Surely a certain amount of money could be voted to erect buildings more suited to human habitation. This experimental farm is the only one in northern Ontario and Quebec and it serves a new agricultural population of nearly a quarter of a million people. I believe the

minister is aware of the fact that the last census show's that the growth in population was greater in northern Ontario than in any other part of the country. I contend this farm should receive more consideration than it has received in the past. I believe the minister will be astonished to learn that there is no adequate barn accommodation on that farm. Everyone knows the kind of weather encountered in that part of the country when the crops are being gathered. With no barn available losses will be incurred in gathering the early crops. Surely it is possible to provide a decent barn.

If the estimates of any department are increased, it should be those of the Department of Agriculture. The settlers in these new sections are entitled to the benefits of an experimental farm. Wonderful work has been done at this farm, work which has proven beneficial to the entire country. An increase in the work of this farm would, I believe, be the best means of taking fifty per cent of our farmers off direct relief. Three years ago the federal government placed a poultryman on this farm. This young man continued to work for three or four months. He gave lectures in all sections of that country in an effort to give the settlers an idea of what could be accomplished by raising poultry. There is a fine domestic market for these products in that section of the country. Many of these settlers went ahead and built hen coops and bought other equipment at considerable expense, but without any explanation whatsoever, either to the man or to the settlers, this poultryman wras withdrawn. Upon making inquiries at the department I was told that this man was fully qualified for the w'ork he was doing, but without any explanation he was withdrawn. If this was done because of economy, I believe it was false economy. Many of these settlers still have uncompleted hen coops which they started on the advice of the federal government. The government is being penny wise and pound foolish when it takes such action as this. All the people in Canada benefit from the work carried on at these experimental farms. I believe the minister is fully acquainted with northern Ontario and Quebec. I am not asking that millions of dollars be expended; all I am suggesting is an expenditure of about $10,000 or $15,000 so that the men who work on this farm can be housed in a decent manner and the administration of the farm may not have to surmount the difficulties it has to face at the moment.

work has many times been the subject of discussion throughout the country. I have been asked how it is that the provinces maintain so many demonstration farms when the dominion maintains experimental as well as demonstration farms. I am fully aware that the experimental farms are not self sustaining, and yet some revenue is produced. Looking at the auditor general's report for the last five years we find that the deficits on our experimental farms amount to $9,000,000. I would ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) to consider that point; he might be able to effect an economy in this regard. I am not finding fault with the management of our experimental farms under either the last administration or the one that held office before that; I believe those farms have done much useful work. But in view of the fact that the work of the provinces and the dominion overlaps, I suggest that the government consider seriously turning the work over to the provinces. I do not mean that the dominion should forsake the work altogether, but I believe it could pay annually a substantial sum of money-nothing like S9.000.000, but perhaps as much as $500,000-to help the provinces carry on the work. In addition, I would give a bonus to experts who have developed many of our cereals and whose horticultural work has been beneficial to the whole dominion. The cost would not be great, but the expenditure would be an incentive to some of these men to complete their work and perhaps to develop something of material benefit to the dominion. There is a feeling throughout Canada that there is too much overlapping, and the dominion government would be well advised to leave the work to the provinces, the officials of which are most familiar with their respective soils and needs.

,Liberal,,Malcolm McLean,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=f748183f-ae06-44a3-9d1a-5802d8e25ea3&Language=E&Section=ALL
1078943,ca.proc.d.1936-02-21.10.96,1936-02-21,b88f8c1a-3837-4be1-8acb-61fedd1a9cc1,ca.m.1363,Mr. GARDINER:,Minister of Agriculture,DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE,,,I heard the remark

made by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader), but I have no records here by which to check the figures, taking it simply as a statement of revenue and expenditure. I should like to point out that it is imposible for anyone to determine whether there has been a loss or a gain through the expenditure on experimental farm work. You cannot simply take the expenditure that is made upon the farms and compare that with the proceeds from what is sold off the farm, because this is not an attempt on the part of the government to run a farm and demonstrate to farmers in the surrounding area that a farm can be run and made a financial success. That is not the intention at all. The intention is rather to carry on research and experimental work, and I would say that the research work carried on which led to the production of Marquis wheat resulted in vastly greater profits to the Dominion of Canada and greater possibilities of paying revenues than could possibly be measured by anything that might be charged up against the farms as a result of any work they did. The experimental farms are there for the purpose of trying to benefit all farmers in Canada and the dominion as a whole. We had in western Canada down to the middle of July last year, for example, one of the finest crops that anyone who has lived in western Canada has ever seen standing in our fields. Looking at that crop one could have asumed that we would harvest one of the greatest crops in bushelage in the history of western Canada. But between the middle and the end of July that crop was practically wiped out of existence over a considerable part of western Canada, all because of the fact that under certain climatic conditions the wheat -which we had sown was subject to rust. We got those climatic conditions, and the result was that our wheat crop was practically wiped out over about one-half of the western provinces. If the development during the last twelve years of a rust resistant wheat results in there being sown in western Canada a wheat with the same qualities for milling purposes as, say, Marquis wheat, and which will produce the same volume per acre as Reward or Marquis wheat, no one can estimate either the deficit or the surplus in the operation of the station at Winnipeg which resulted in the production of that wheat. I would not attempt, therefore, to justify or to explain any statement to the effect that nine million dollars had been lost through the operation of our experimental farms.

1078982,ca.proc.d.1936-02-21.10.135,1936-02-21,b88f8c1a-3837-4be1-8acb-61fedd1a9cc1,ca.m.1363,Mr. GARDINER:,Minister of Agriculture,DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE,,,Fairs have been classified into A class fairs and B class fairs in accordance with the work that is carried on by them. 1078992,ca.proc.d.1936-02-21.10.145,1936-02-21,b88f8c1a-3837-4be1-8acb-61fedd1a9cc1,ca.m.1363,Mr. GARDINER:,Minister of Agriculture,DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE,,,We have attempted to
be as generous as possible with class B fairs as compared with previous years, with the exception of last year.

I should like to make a general statement to the committee as to our policy in connection with these fairs. Since coming into the department I have found some difficulty in arriving at a conclusion as to whether certain fairs should be given these grants. Quite different practices are followed in different parts of Canada, and I have asked the head of the branch concerned to visit different parts of the country and look into the matter. Already he has been in the maritimes; he has visited certain organizations in the central part of Canada and has been in Winnipeg, where he met those interested in the promotion of exhibitions. At the moment, however, we are not in a position to arrive at a final decision as to what ought to be done. My desire is to have established for the payment of grants to these different classes of fairs right across Canada a standard to which we can adhere and which will apply in an equitable way to these fairs wherever they may be held, at the same time giving, from an agricultural point of view, the greatest possible service to the people. With that end in view during the coming year we intend to investigate these different fairs right across Canada in order to try to arrive at some system of regulation and some method of paying the grants that will be generally satisfactory. So at the next session we hope to bring down some standard upon which this can be based, and it can be discussed then in the light of the information that has been gathered. At the moment I do not fee' that the information I have been able to gaiher since coming into the department has put me in a position to arrive at a satisfactory decision with regard to this matter; I feel I should know more about it before coming to a definite conclusion.

There are one or two things, however, that I think should be mentioned. We find that there is more overlapping as between the dominion and the provinces in this activity than in perhaps any other, without having accurate information as to what the qther departments are doing. For example we find that in one province we were offering a maximum grant of $3,000 to class B fairs while the province was paying $1,000 to the same fairs. We feel that there should be some cooperation between the provinces and the federal government in arriving at a decision as to what the grant ought to be, and that before we arrive at a decision as to that we should know what is being paid by the various provinces. We pay the same grant all across Canada, but different provinces pay different grants, and we do not think this makes for equality of assistance to the different fairs. So we intend to gather all available information as to what is being done by the provinces and as to what are the needs of these various exhibitions and fairs; then we will bring down with regard to the payment of grants some method or policy which we hope will be satisfactory right across Canada.

1078993,ca.proc.d.1936-02-21.10.146,1936-02-21,31caaca0-4621-41f8-bfe9-f6857896dea1,ca.m.5322,Mr. LEADER:,,DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE,,,I should like to commend

the minister for his action in making a general review of the fair situation in Canada. After ten years of exhibition w'ork on the fair circuits of the dominion almost from coast to coast I can say that I do not know of any other place where there is more confusion, at least to the exhibitor than at these fairs, and we must acknowledge that without the exhibitors the fairs could not carry on. One of the greatest handicaps and most discouraging features about the fairs is the lack of uniformity in their prize lists and classifications. For instance some fairs will call for an aged herd, a bull and four females, all over two years of age. This necessitates a man carrying two cows and two two-year olds, and so on. Then the next fair he goes to he will be required to bring perhaps two females and a bull, or perhaps a graded herd which calls for a bull, cow a two year old, a yearling and a calf. When a man goes to the expense of getting a herd , of cattle fitted for exhibition-and it is considerable expense -he wants to get all the prize money he can or he is out of pocket. This lack of uniformity in prize lists means that an exhibitor has to carry far more animals than he should have to carry. That is expensive. It acts as a hardship and a discouragement to young breeders in this way, that when an exhibitor carries two or more in one class he is going to exhibit them, and an experienced breeder

may take perhaps first, second and third, while the farmer who may have just as good an animal but not in as fit condition, gets only the tail end of the prize money. He has paid freight and the result is that he goes home out of pocket. This discourages the young breeder and he does not continue exhibiting. I know dozens of cases where this has happened. I think exhibitors should be discouraged from carrying more than one animal in each class, and I believe uniformity in prize lists would have that effect.

I am glad the minister has seen fit to undertake this investigation. I wish to take this opportunity of saying that I have no fault to find with the Hon. 1079034,ca.proc.d.1936-02-21.11.2,1936-02-21,da1e46fc-5b99-4c79-850a-a1cf6cbe555f,ca.m.7872,Mr. J. G. ROSS (Moose Jaw):,,RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT,,,"Mr. Speaker, when I adjourned the debate last night on Bill No. 2, I did so because I thought many hon. members from western Canada would want to speak on the bill when they realized the importance of it to the people of that section of the country. This bill does not ask for a change in railway rates; it asks only to have a full application of the Crowsnest rates westward as well as eastward. When in 1897 the Crowsnest rate was first brought into effect commodities shipped eastward from western Canada were given a stated rate under the Crowsnest pass agreement. At that time the rate for grain and flour was set at three cents below the regular rate of that time, and the agreement was that the rate would remain in effect for all time.
Later, during the war, that rate was suspended. In 1925 it was again put into effect by a government headed by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). Some
Railway Act-Rates on Grain

people have argued that if we were to pass the bill we would affect the whole freight rate structure of Canada. That is not so. When by order in council in 1925 the government instructed the board of railway commissioners to look into this matter they asked that freight rates be equalized in the different parts of Canada. I have in my hand order in council P.C. 886 which at that time dealt with the Crowsnest pass agreement. I am going to read only that part of it which affects the bill. Speaking of the Crowsnest pass agreement, by order in council the government of that day said:

The committee observe that the agreement in question was made at a time when the Canadian Pacific Railway Company was the only company having a through line of railway extending through the prairie provinces and British Columbia, and before the creation of the board for the control of railway rates under the provisions of the Railway Act of 1903, and subsequent acts. And further, that the underlying purpose of the rate control inaugurated by the Railway Act of 1903 was to do away as far as possible with all unjust discriminations and undue preferences, and to secure a fair and reasonable rate structure, which, under substantially similar circumstances and conditions would be equal in its application to all persons and localities.

The committee are of the opinion that the policy of equalization of freight rates should be recognized to the fullest possible extent as being the only means of dealing equitably with all parts of Canada, and as being the method best calculated to facilitate the interchange of commodities between the various portions of the dominion, as well as the encouragement of industry and agriculture, and the development of export trade.
Then, in another paragraph I find the following:

The committee are further of the opinion that as the production and export of grain and flour forms one of the chief assets of the dominion, and in order to encourage the further development of the great grain growing provinces in the west, on which development the future of Canada in large measure depends, it is desirable that the maximum cost of the transportation of these products should be determined and known, and therefore are of opinion that the maximum established for rates on grain and flour, as at present in force under the Crowsnest pass agreement, should not be exceeded.

The Crowsnest pass agreement in effect to-day between western points and Fort William and Port Arthur is a rate that carries grain, whether for export or for domestic purposes, to Fort William and Port Arthur. For many years I have been shipping grain from western Canada, and I can bill any kind of grain to my order at Fort William or Port Arthur, and there take delivery of the grain myself, or deliver it to anyone to whom I see fit. At the time this order in council

was passed the government intended that the maximum rate should apply west, as well as east, and therefore if their intention had been carried out by the board of railway commissioners of that day rates on all grain and flour to British Columbia ports would have been the Crowsnest pass rates, whether for export or for domestic purposes. However, the board of railway commissioners of that day did not carry out the intention of the government. Let me read from a speech delivered by the then and now leader of the government (Mr. Mackenzie King), on this point:
I would say to the house and the country that if this government remains in office it will not take the view of the order in council which my right hon. friend takes-
Upon that occasion he was replying to the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen.

-but -will regard that order in council as a direction to the railway commission as to how it expects this policy to be worked out, and will see that the policy is worked out in accordance with the terms of the order in council. The order in council sets out the government policy. It is a direction to the railway commission to equalize rates. That direction indicates how this government expects this policy of equalization to be worked out. And I would remind hon. members that there remains, as the commission itself well knows, an appeal from the commission to the governor in council with respect to matters of railway rates. This government has stated what its policy is with respect to the equalization of rates, and unless that policy is carried out in accordance -with its intention'-if this government is in office *when the question comes up -and I have not the least doubt it will be- it will take care to see that the policy is carried out in the spirit and intent of the letter as expressed in the order in council itself.

The intention expressed in the order in council was that the Crowsnest pass rates should be extended to British Columbia ports -the same Crowsnest rates that were given to Fort William and Port Arthur. Therefore I claim that for the past ten years a right belonging to the people of the western provinces has been denied them by a ruling of the board of railway commissioners. This is a very important matter at this time, now that the trade treaty with the United States is in operation. Under that treaty it will be found that feed grains are allowed into the United States under a duty of ten per cent ad valorem. This means that feed grain shipped to Vancouver, Victoria, New Westminster or Prince Rupert can go into the United States, to Oregon, Washington and California, where there is a very large market for it. If this amendment is adopted it will mean that anyone will be able to take delivery of grain at terminal elevators in the western
Railway Act-Rates on Grain

ports. It does not mean that this rate will be applied to shipments to local points, but it does mean that at the terminal elevators on the coast anyone may take delivery of grain shipped under the Crowsnest pass rate.

As I have said, Mr. Speaker, in this amendment we are not asking for any change at all in the rate structure. No one can raise a quid pro quo in this regard, because this is a right we had under the Crowsnest pass agreement, and it is a right for which every western man in the house should stand up and fight, because it means an expanding market for the grain we produce on the prairies. I hope that when other western men in this chamber have spoken to the bill the government will seriously consider amending the act in this regard. It may be necessary, first of all, to send the bill to the railway committee, where all the facts may be gone into. Our position is that we have only a portion of the Crowsnest rate westward, only that portion for export, but that eastward we have the full Crowsnest rate that is spoken of in this order in council. By this bill my hon. friend is endeavouring to give back to us in western Canada a right which we have been denied for the past ten years.

would have no desire to speak on this measure at this time except for one fact. Ten years ago in the house I recall some of my friends from British Columbia proposing a resolution asking that help be given to the poultry keepers of that province, and they made a strong argument for their case, pointing out among other things that poultry keepers there were handicapped by a climate somewhat harsher than that enjoyed by some of their competitors in Georgia, Florida and other southern states. To me their argument was not convincing, because I well knew that nature had provided poultry with protection against cold weather, but as far as I knew nature had not provided any ventilating apparatus for poultry kept in hot climates. Therefore I was regretfully obliged to tell them that I could not support their appeal for higher protection on eggs and poultry products. Naturally I had to look further into the question and see whether there was something else that might be a handicap to feeders of poultry and other live stock in the great western maritime province. I formed the opinion at that time, and
Railway Act-Rates on Grain

expressed it, that if they were able to buy their supplies wholesale and get them laid down at a lower freight rate than they were then paying this would help them a good deal more than if they ware to secure some artificial protection. As I say, hon. members who at that time were representing British Columbia made a very eloquent appeal for that industry, and some went so far as to say that the poultry industry was dying and that unless it got this additional protection it could not last much longer. But figures given by other hon. gentlemen in the same debate showed that British Columbia was turning out a tremendous production of eggs right along, an increase of something like one hundred per cent in a few years; my memory is not certain as to the precise figure, but poultry production had been increasing very greatly.

I went further and assured my friends from British Columbia that if they should introduce either a resolution, or better perhaps a bill, providing for lowering freight rates on grain and feed stuffs going into that province from the prairies I should be glad to lend them what support I could, sitting at that time on the government side of the house, as I am now, and they sitting on the opposition side. I recall very distinctly that on the occasion of that debate I was reproached by the then right hon. leader of the opposition, who made the statement that one of the leading ministers on this side had said that no reduction of freight rates could be given. But this was not a general reduction we were pleading for; it was a specific reduction to do away with what many looked upon as an economic injustice to a large group of people in Canada. It may be that I do not attach quite so much importance to it from the standpoint of the prairie farmer as some of those do who have spoken before me, because the total amount of grain that would go from Saskatchewan or Manitoba to the western coast to be used in domestic consumption would not be very large; the percentage of the whole crop that was shipped in that way would not be great. We realize that the railroads of this country made a very reasonable bargain with the government of the day when they arranged for the Crowsnest pass agreement, but that was at a time when very little grain was being consumed locally by way of feed stuffs, very little being used for stock within the dominion. When the Crowsnest pass arrangement was negotiated nearly forty years ago, localities that are now asking for cheaper rates on grain were not producing live stock to anything like the extent they do now, and in most cases they were probably producing a large percentage of the food required within their own borders, so that domestic freight rates were not nearly so important as they have since become.

A few years after the discussion to which I referred in my opening remarks I enjoyed the pleasure of a trip in part of British Columbia, through the Fraser valley. By the kind invitation of the organized boards of trade of that great valley, conveyed to members for the three prairie provinces through the courtesy and kindness of the hon. member for what was then, I think, the constituency of Fraser Valley, I took part in a trip up and down through that district for about three days. I and those who went with me had an opportunity to visit poultry farms, dairy farms, general farms and farms where they made a specialty of growing rose bushes and many other special products of that great province. On many occasions in the course of that visit, speaking to farmers who were engaged in the dairy business, particularly, in the poultry business, I asked what their greatest handicaps were. I do not need to tell the house that none of them complained of the wonderful climate they enjoyed in British Columbia. That was one thing upon which they were unanimous: they were under no handicap as far as climate was concerned.

Railway rates are in a somewhat chaotic condition. I do not think they were ever made at all; like Topsy, they ""just growed;"" they grew into a state of confusion. PELLETIER (Peace River):,,RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT,,,Mr. Speaker, I did not equip myself with the necessary details to speak authoritatively on this bill to-night, but so far as the principle of it is concerned some glaring inequalities have come to my attention, and for that reason alone I should like to draw two or three facts to the attention of hon. members.
An hon. member speaking a few moments ago spoke of the equalization of freight rates. Apparently, even though we recog-
Railway Act-Rates on Grain

nize that the agricultural products of western Canada constitute the bulk of the wealth produced in the west, we find that because of their geographical position our western people are discriminated against. There is a great deal more to be said about the equalization of freight rates, and the day will come when it will be recognized that as a matter of justice we shall have to equalize our freight rates.

One point that particularly struck me was that so far as eastern Canada is concerned there is a single freight rate, and we call that the rate to eastern Canada, but when we ship grain westward we find that there are two Tates, an export and a domestic rate. The other evening when an hon. member was speaking another hon. gentleman interrupted to suggest that the railway companies were carrying grain at what they call the export rate to pay their out-of-pocket expenses. Of course, it is all very well not to lose money in doing business but the difference between what is called the export rate and the domestic rate is so great that surely we in western Canada should not be expected to bear entirely the burden of this discrimination. Not very long ago, simply because of drought conditions in the western states of the United States there appeared in the Canadian tariff books a feed grain rate to that republic to enable feed grain to be shipped to those drought areas. As I said at the outset, Mr. Speaker, I am not equipped with the necessary details to give comparisons of freight rates this evening, but I do know that feed grain rate was very favourable and it was established simply to help those people who had suffered from drought conditions.

It is admitted in the house that when we in western Canada ship our grain it is mostly for export; that not a very large quantity is consumed locally. That being the case we must take it for granted that the bulk of the grain of western Canada is being exported, and we find that British Columbia is really being discriminated against because of this difference between domestic and export rates. I can see no reason why those two rates should exist.
I find by the explanatory note that subsection 5 of section 325, to be amended, reads in part as follows:

-and to change and alter rates as changing conditions or cost of transportation may from time to time require, shall not be limited or in any manner affected by the provisions of any act of the parliament of Canada.
Note those words: ""Change and alter rates as changing conditions or cost of transportation may from time to time require."" A great deal

of domestic grain is to-day consumed in British Columbia because of the growth of the poultry industry in that province, and I submit for the consideration of hon. members that apart entirely from the benefit which has been derived by western farmers we should consider the needs of this ever-growing industry in British Columbia.

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, as a matter of fairness I can see no reason why the people of the west should be discriminated against by having two rates apply to them when only one rate applies to eastern Canada, and as a Canadian I would simply say that on grounds of fairness and equality I am entirely in support of this bill.

Mr. A. MacG. YOUNG (Saskatoon): Mr. Speaker, I rise to-night to say just a few words on this bill. In the first place I should like to congratulate its sponsor (Mr. Reid) upon the excellence of the arguments which he advanced. His arguments were clear; they were logical; they were forceful, and they were thorough.

One point which impressed me more than anything else was the fact that his argument had a ring of sincerity, and behind it all there seemed to be the feeling which he was expressing on behalf of the people of British Columbia, that they were suffering a real injustice.

It has been said that the House of Commons, constituted as it is, is not the proper place to discuss the whole complex matter of the freight rate structure, and I believe we are all agreed on that. But may I suggest that it was not the board of railway commissioners that settled the Crowsnest pass agreement. That particular part of the freight rate structure was settled by the house, and it seems to me that if what the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) said to-night is correct-and I have no doubt of its correctness-it was ordered that any discrimination between east and west should be removed. The hon. gentleman went on further to say that grain could be moved to Fort William and Port Arthur and further east and sold there for domestic consumption, and that the rate on such grain for domestic consumption would be the same as the export rate. As I understand the law and the rules and regulations and orders in council that have been passed, it was intended that the same thing should apply to grain and flour moving westward. Now if that be true, what is the situation? This simply means that the domestic rate on grain and flour moving to our western ports should be the same as the export rate.
Railway Act-Rates on Grain

The hon. member for New Westminster the other evening gave to the house the export and domestic rates, and there does seem to be a very great discrimination. If parliament did order a certain rate, and the board of railway commissioners does not see fit to put that rate into effect, I suggest that parliament or perhaps the government has a duty to perform. I remember very well, as a former member of the house, speaking on the question of discrimination in freight rates. When the Crowsnest pass agreement was introduced it applied not only to the original lines of railway existing at the time but to all other railways constructed thereafter. It so happened that in wesitern Canada on certain lines of railway there had been a discrimination of about two cents per hundred pounds on grain moving eastward, and the law of this country directed that the board should see that all these discriminations were removed. These discriminations were not removed immediately. From western Canada we sent east some of our ablest lawyers who argued this case time and time again. Some of us came to parliament and we found that this discrimination still existed. I remember that I advanced in the house the best argument of which I was capable against these discriminations. I even went so far as to say that if the board of railway commissioners did not see fit to carry out the laws over which they had jurisdiction, then we should see that the board was removed. The hon. member for Outremont (Mr. Vien), who spoke in the house the other night, was a member of the board at that time. If he were in his place this evening I would have pleasure in stating that he was one of those who believed that the discrimination should be removed. The fight was carried on to such an extent that the board of railway commissioners removed the discrimination.

If I am correct, and if the hon. member for Moose Jaw is correct in stating that there exists to-day a discrimination which is not intended under the law, I submit it is the duty of the board of railway commissioners to see that the discrimination is removed. One of the curses of this country has been the restrictions placed upon trade. Restriction of trade may be caused by too high a tariff; it may be caused by a manipulation of the tariff; it may be caused by manipulation of exchange or in various other ways. There is still one further way in which it may be caused, and that is by an unfair railway rate structure. I believe that to be true in the case of gasoline; I believe it to be true of the commodities which are the subject matter of this bill. If it is true, then we as a parliament

have a duty to perform. If there are injustices, we should see that they are removed. What is this House of Commons for; what is this parliament for, except to make laws in the interests of the people of Canada as a whole? The people of British Columbia feel that they are suffering under a heavy handicap because they cannot get their poultry and stock feed at a price which seems to be fair. As the hon. gentleman (Mr. Reid) said the other night, our wheat can be shipped to Vancouver, then to Japan and reshipped back again to Vancouver for twenty-five cents per ton less than it costs to ship it to Vancouver under the domestic rate. I believe I have remembered the figures correctly. If they are right, surely something is wrong with our freight tariff. I rise to support this bill because I believe an injustice exists. My further observation is that we as a parliament should see that any injustice which does exist is removed.

HOWE (Minister of Railways and Canals):,Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals,RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT,,,Mr. Speaker, this bill refers to a matter now on appeal to the governor in council. A case covering rates on the commodities mentioned in the bill was presented to the board of railway commissioners in January, 1935. A decision was rendered and I think the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), on behalf of certain British Columbia interests took the appeal himself to the governor in council. That being so, I think it would be manifestly unfair for me to express any opinion as to the merits or demerits of the subject matter of the bill. I can assure my hon. friend that this appeal will be heard at the earliest possible date, probably shortly after the completion of this session. At that time the evidence heard by the commission will be studied, the representations of my hon. friend will be weighed against representations which may be made by other interested parties, and I am sure that a fair decision will be reached. As I say, it would under these circumstances, be quite improper for me to express an opinion of the bill, but I do not think it would be out of order for me to say something about rate making.

It has been stated two or three times during the debate that parliament is not the proper place to discuss railway rates as these matters are very technical. I know I am not qualified to discuss them and I doubt whether any hon. member is qualified to discuss the pros and cons of this intricate problem. This debate seems to indicate that the impression of everyone is that rates should be lower. That is quite natural and I would be much surprised if anyone other than the Minister
Supply-Railways-Hudson Bay
of Railways stood up in the house and suggested that it might be a good thing to have higher rates. However speeches of this kind give the people an idea that the railroads are being very unfair.

I might mention one or two matters which perhaps will show the other side of the question. A good deal was said about domestic and export rates on grain to Fort William being the same. Why Fort William? I would point out that Fort William is located

The grain that has been loaded at Churchill has been loaded by Louis Wolfe and Company, who are the principal stevedoring agents in Montreal for account of the steamship company. They naturally do not bring all their stevedores there from Montreal, but the superintendent is there and from the men at the port he is furnished with sufficient labour to do the work as and when required. We simply turn the men over to Louis Wolfe and Company and charge them the ordinary rate of pay of the men plus thirty-five per cent to cover transportation in and out and other charges that we have to pay against those men. The results have been fairly satisfactory. The cost of loading grain in Vancouver is 82 a thousand bushels; at Churchill it is $4 a thousand; it is also 84 a thousand in the port of New York, so that really stevedoring charges at Churchill are not sufficiently high to interfere very much with the traffic.

1079148,ca.proc.d.1936-02-21.12.99,1936-02-21,81e9d110-f6b1-4643-a4a5-d110dba9135f,ca.m.7827,Mr. MOTHERWELL:,,RAILWAYS AND CANALS,,,I think it is generally recognized that all through the ages new trade routes had great difficulty in' getting established, because they had to compete with older established routes. In addition to that the Hudson Bay railway has had no great pressure upon it because in the last four or five years the crops have been light and the peak load did not demand it at that particular time. Hence the wheat and cattle pool, were the only bodies that made any effort to use the route in spite of the extortionate insurance rates that have been charged since its inception.

I do not know what insurance rates were charged on the Panama canal at the outset, but I remember it was with great misgivings that the first few boats went through the Panama. Probably the minister has some information as to how long it took to start wheat rolling through that canal and how many cargoes went through in the first, second, third and fourth years. I remember quite well there was no very pronounced flow of wheat until after the Crowsnest rates were extended to the Pacific, and then the quantity of wheat carried via the Panama increased very rapidly.
If we should have a similar experience in reducing insurance rates on the northern route I have no doubt that the Hudson Bay railway would be very much more used than it is.

I wonder whether the minister could tell us if the freight rate is also charged on the excess mileage that it takes to get to Churchill over and above what it should have taken had we gone directly there. Does the minister know? The Hudson Bay railway was built through an engineering blunder with the idea of going to Nelson, an impossible port, and was diverted to Churchill, occasioning about forty or fifty miles more mileage than if it had gone directly to Churchill in the beginning.

If the freight rate is charged on that excess forty or fifty miles it is an unjust charge against that wheat. Why should farmers pay the freight on a joy .ride of forty miles rendered necessary by somebody's blunder in going to Nelson first? The minister may have information to answer some of the ques-

freight rates is that the rate from Winnipeg to Port Arthur and that from the port at Churchill have been equalized. They are roughly the same distance; I do not think the difference is a matter of forty or fifty miles. I think this was done in. a more or less arbitrary way. The Crowsnest pass rates apply from the Pas in the case of Churchill and from Winnipeg in the case of Port Arthur So I do not think there is any detrimental effect from the fact that the railroad does not go in an absolutely straight line.

My recollection is that the elevator in Vancouver was completed in 1916, and that except for one test cargo no grain moved from there until 1922, when I think two cargoes were loaded. Then in 1923 the elevator handled 53 million bushels, so it came into its own very quickly after some seven years.

1079171,ca.proc.d.1936-02-21.12.122,1936-02-21,c0217f54-28e5-4cd6-8ce3-4d47e7475495,ca.m.4448,Mr. CRERAR:,Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs,RAILWAYS AND CANALS,,,The hon. member for

Saskatoon (Mr. Young) has been good enough to refer to me as a former Minister of Railways who was interested in the development of this port. My experience as Minister of Railways was rather limited due to the fact that the right hon. gentleman who leads the opposition (Mr. Bennett) put out of business, not only the government of that day, but me as well. I am interested in the development of the Hudson bay route because all of this railway lies within the riding I represent at the present time. It is a fact well known to all hon. gentlemen, and certainly to those from western Canada, that the building of the Hudson Bay railway, the development of the port at Churchill and the route across to Europe have constituted a matter of vital concern and interest to the people of western Canada for a great many years. I can recall having made many speeches on this subject when I was in the house many years ago.

I know there are in eastern Canada many critics of this development, and I was interested in the question asked by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Spence) as to the total cost up to the present time of the whole development. It is true that this has cost $53,000,000, but it is only fair to say that included in that amount is the money that was expended on the development of Port Nelson. When the late Mr. Cochrane was Minister of Railways over twenty years ago, the government of that day undertook the completion of the road and fixed upon Port Nelson as the terminus. Notwithstanding any criticism that may have been made of it I do not think any mistake was made when the terminus was moved from Port Nelson to Churchill. Port Nelson had an open roadstead and would never have made a successful port, but several millions of dollars were spent before it was finally abandoned. Churchill has one of the best natural harbours in the world, being completely protected from storms of all kinds. I was there on July 1 last and at that time the river and bay were clear. There was some drift ice along the shore, but nothing which an icebreaker could not get through. Although the port is at the present time open for navigation for only about two months in the year, this is because of high insurance rates, and my settled conviction is that the day will come, and before many years, when the port will be used for three and a half or four months in the year. I think all the available data-and there is a good deal of it-goes to substantiate that view.
Reference has been made to the Bright Fan incident, but I think I am correct in saying

that the inquiry into the sinking of that ship disclosed that it was at least sixty miles off its course and that practically everyone, including the captain, was intoxicated when the accident took place. I know my predecessor from Churchill constituency expressed the view in the house that the Bright Fan had been deliberately sunk, but whether that is true I cannot say. We all know the effect of an incident of that kind upon underwriters. I have no doubt they hold that as a black mark against the development of the route. Personally, I find myself a good deal in sympathy with the view expressed by the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly), and I assure the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Young) that I shall not forget the admonition he has given me to-night. If I cannot prevail upon the Minister of Railways (Mr. Howe), who is I know wholly sympathetic to the development of the route, and if I cannot touch the stony heart of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), it will not be for lack of carrying out the injunction he has given me.

,Liberal,,Walter Adam Tucker,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=4d785391-75cd-4998-a9da-636344a54e3d&Language=E&Section=ALL
1079195,ca.proc.d.1936-02-21.12.146,1936-02-21,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals,RAILWAYS AND CANALS,,,That is purely a matter of government policy. Of course the matter is restricted in some ways. We have treaty obligations with the United States which require that tolls for Canadian and American shipping must be equal. Tied to that are treaty relations with favoured nation coun-

tries, which provide that their shipping must be on a basis equal to that of the United States. Possibly the only countries not covered are Germany and Holland, and if we put them on a different basis we would be in trouble.

The matter of tolls for passing through the Welland canal is connected with government policy. Until 1904 tolls were charged, but at that time an order in council was passed which provided that as a matter of government policy no tolls should be charged on the canal. I have not gone into the matter very carefully, but I am not sure that the time is not near when we might examine the situation once more and decide whether tolls should be imposed. I am simply making that observation, without having looked into the facts.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1079196,ca.proc.d.1936-02-21.12.147,1936-02-21,b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f,ca.m.6164,Mr. BENNETT:,Leader of the Official Opposition,RAILWAYS AND CANALS,,,When the minister is looking into the matter he might find it interesting to get the state papers of the United States and read the story of the construction of the Soo canal. We did endeavour to give a preference to our own ships. We were giving them a rebate when they came to Montreal, coming through the Soo canal with cargoes bound for Montreal. The Americans protested and ultimately, as will be recalled, they built the American Soo canal. As the matter now stands, the reason the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier removed the tolls in 1904- and I believe the minister had the correct date-was that they imposed an additional burden upon the grain growers of the west; that is the real reason. As every ship, whether American or Canadian, or one of a country enjoying favoured nation treatment, had to pay a toll, it followed that that meant just an additional burden upon ships which brought cargoes from the west to Montreal. If it was a Canadian ship it meant that freight charges were enhanced, as happened in connection with other ships as well.

The real reason of this arrangement, one which some people thought was misunderstood philanthropy, was really an effort on our part to lessen the charges on the movement of wheat from Fort William and Port Arthur to Montreal, destined for export to the markets of the world. I recall that I was pressed very strongly to deal with this matter of tolls, and I am sure the minister has probabaly had representations made to him in the same sense. We must remember however that, to begin with, there are treaty obligations with the United States, and we cannot discriminate against their ships. Then there are favoured nations, who stand in exactly the same position, and lastly there is the economic feature of the matter namely, the additional cost per
Supply-Canals
bushel which would be involved in the movement of grain for export from the head of the lakes to Montreal.

1079280,ca.proc.d.1936-02-21.12.231,1936-02-21,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals,RAILWAYS AND CANALS,,,In 1934-35 Port Colborne handled 14,380,000 bushels. Churchill in that year handled 3,9/64,000 bushels. The nature of the operation at Port Colborne is the cheapest of any known elevator where it unloads from a boat and discharges to a boat. An elevator at an ocean terminal is quite different. It receives cars; there is a cleaning operation involved, and there is also an extensive gallery equipment for loading boats requiring quite a large operating staff. An elevator such as that at Churchill is the most expensive type. I think my hon. friend, in trying to compare the two, is comparing two very unequal things, and the charges are quite easily accounted for.
